source_text: Ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν αὐτῶν τὰ σοφὰ τοῖς ἀραχνείοις ὑφάσμασιν ἔοικεν, οἷς ὅταν μὲν κώνωψ, ἢ μυῖα, ἤ τι τῶν παραπλησίως τούτοις ἀσθενῶν ἐνσχεθῇ, κατα δεθέντα κρατεῖται· ἐπειδὰν δὲ τῶν ἰσχυροτέρων τι ζῴων ἐγγίσῃ, αὐτό τε ῥᾳδίως διεκπίπτει, καὶ τὰ ἀδρανῆ ὑφάσμα τα διέρρηξε καὶ ἠφάνισε. 6.7 Καὶ οὐκ ἐπὶ τούτων ἵστανται μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧν ἡ προαίρεσις ἑκάστου ἡμῶν κυρία (λέγω δὴ, τῶν ἐπιτηδευμάτων ἀρετῆς ἢ κακίας), καὶ τούτων τὰς αἰτίας τοῖς οὐρανίοις συνάπτουσιν. Οἷς τὸ ἀντιλέγειν ἄλλως μὲν καταγέλαστον, διὰ δὲ τὸ προκατέχεσθαι τοὺς πολλοὺς τῇ ἀπάτῃ, ἀναγκαῖον ἴσως μὴ σιωπῇ παρελθεῖν. Πρῶτον μὲν οὖν ἐκεῖνο αὐτοὺς ἐρωτήσωμεν, εἰ μὴ ἐφ' ἑκάστης ἡμέρας μυριάκις ἀμείβεται τῶν ἀστέρων τὰ σχήματα; Ἀεικίνητοι γὰρ ὄντες οἱ πλανῆται λεγόμενοι, καὶ οἱ μὲν θᾶττον ἐπικατα λαμβάνοντες ἀλλήλους, οἱ δὲ βραδυτέρας τὰς περιόδους ποιούμενοι, ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς ὥρας πολλάκις καὶ ὁρῶσιν ἀλλήλους καὶ ἀποκρύπτονται, μεγίστην τε ἔχει δύμανιν ἐν ταῖς γενέσεσι τὸ ἢ παρὰ ἀγαθοποιοῦ ἐφορᾶσθαι, ἢ κακοποιοῦ, ὡς αὐτοὶ λέγουσι. Καὶ πολλάκις καθ' ὃν ἐπεμαρτύρει ὁ ἀγαθοποιὸς ἀστὴρ τὸν καιρὸν οὐκ ἐξευρόντες, παρὰ τὴν ἑνὸς τῶν λεπτοτάτων ἄγνοιαν, ὡς ἐν τῷ κακοδαιμονήματι αὐτὸν κείμενον ἀπεγράψαντο. Τοῖς γὰρ αὐτῶν ἐκείνων συγχρήσασθαι ῥήμασιν ἀναγκάζομαι. Ἐν δὴ τοῖς τοιούτοις λόγοις πολὺ μὲν τὸ ἀνόητον, πολλαπλάσιον δὲ τὸ ἀσεβές. Οἱ γὰρ κακοποιοὶ τῶν ἀστέρων τῆς ἑαυτῶν πονηρίας ἐπὶ τὸν ποιήσαντα αὐτοὺς τὴν αἰτίαν μετατιθέασιν. Εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἐκ φύσεως αὐτῶν τὸ κακὸν, ὁ δημιουργὸς ἔσται τοῦ κακοῦ ποιητής· εἰ δὲ προαιρέσει κακύνονται, πρῶτον μὲν ἔσται ζῷα προαιρετικὰ, λελυμέναις καὶ αὐτοκρατορικαῖς ταῖς ὁρμαῖς κεχρημένα· ὃ μανίας ἐστὶν ἐπέκεινα καταψεύδεσθαι τῶν ἀψύχων. Ἔπειτα πόσον τὸ ἄλογον, τὸ κακὸν καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν μὴ κατὰ τὴν ἀξίαν διανέμειν ἑκάστῳ, ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ ἐν τῷδε τῷ τόπῳ γέγονεν, ἀγαθοποιὸν ὑπάρχειν, καὶ ἐπειδὴ ὑπὸ τοῦδε ὁρᾶται, κακοποιὸν γίνεσθαι τὸν αὐτόν· καὶ ἐπειδὰν πάλιν μικρόν τι παρεκκλίνῃ τοῦ σχήματος, εὐθὺς τῆς κακίας ἐπιλανθάνεσθαι; Καὶ ταῦτα μὲν εἰς τοσοῦτον. Εἰ δὲ καθ' ἕκαστον ἀκαριαῖον τοῦ χρόνου ἐπ' ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο μεθαρμόζονται σχῆμα, ἐν δὲ ταῖς μυρίαις ταύταις μεταβολαῖς, πολλάκις τῆς ἡμέρας, οἱ τῶν βασιλικῶν γενέσεων ἀποτελοῦνται σχηματισμοὶ, διὰ τί οὐκ ἐφ' ἑκάστης ἡμέρας γεννῶνται βασιλεῖς; ἢ διὰ τί ὅλως πατρικαὶ παρ' αὐτοῖς εἰσι βασιλείας διαδοχαί; Οὐ δήπου γὰρ ἕκαστος τῶν βασιλέων παρατετηρημένως εἰς τὸ βασιλικὸν τῶν ἀστέρων σχῆμα τοῦ ἰδίου υἱοῦ τὴν γένεσιν ἐναρμόζει. Τίς γὰρ ἀνθρώπων κύριος τοῦ τοιούτου; Πῶς οὖν Ὀζίας ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰωάθαμ; Ἰωάθαμ τὸν ἌχαζἌχαζ τὸν Ἐζεκίαν; καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐν τούτοις δουλικῇ συνέτυχεν ὥρᾳ γενέσεως; Ἔπειτα εἰ καὶ τῶν κατὰ κακίαν καὶ ἀρετὴν ἐνεργημάτων οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ ἐφ' ἡμῖν εἰσὶν αἱ ἀρχαὶ, ἀλλ' ἐκ τῆς γενέσεως αἱ ἀνάγκαι, περιττοὶ μὲν οἱ νομοθέται, τὰ πρακτέα ἡμῖν καὶ τὰ φευκτὰ διορίζοντες, περιττοὶ δὲ καὶ οἱ δικασταὶ, ἀρετὴν τιμῶντες, καὶ πονηρίαν κολάζοντες. Οὐ γὰρ τοῦ κλέπτου τὸ ἀδίκημα· οὐδὲ τοῦ φονέως· ᾧ γε οὐδὲ βουλομένῳ δυνατὸν ἦν κρατεῖν τῆς χειρὸς, διὰ τὸ ἀναπόδραστον τῆς ἐπὶ τὰς πράξεις αὐτὸν κατεπειγούσης ἀνάγκης.
thought_title: Astrology's webs and the absurdity of fate
orientation: Basil is refuting astrology, having just shown that the zodiac signs' supposed characters are borrowed from animals; now he turns to the astrologers' claims about the stars governing human choices and actions.
pass_a_gloss: But these wise things of theirs are like spider webs, in which whenever a gnat or a fly or one of the similarly weak creatures is caught, being bound it is overpowered; but whenever one of the stronger animals approaches, it both easily escapes through, and tears apart and destroys the weak webs. And they do not stop at these things only, but also the things of which the choice of each of us is master (I mean, of the pursuits of virtue or vice), also the causes of these they attach to the heavenly bodies. To contradict them in other respects is ridiculous, but because the many are already held fast by the deception, it is perhaps necessary not to pass by in silence. First then let us ask them this: do not the configurations of the stars change ten thousand times each day? For the so-called planets are always in motion, and some overtake one another more quickly, others make their circuits more slowly, and at the same hour they often both see one another and are hidden from one another, and it has the greatest power in nativities to be watched over by a beneficent star or by a maleficent one, as they themselves say. And often, not having found the moment at which the beneficent star was bearing witness, because of ignorance of one of the most minute points, they recorded him as lying in the evil fortune. For I am compelled to use their own words. In such arguments there is much folly, and far more impiety. For the maleficent stars transfer the cause of their own wickedness to the one who made them. For if their evil is from nature, the creator will be the maker of evil; but if they are made evil by choice, first they will be creatures with choice, using free and self-governing impulses; which is beyond madness to falsely attribute to soulless things. Then how great is the irrationality, not to distribute evil and good to each according to worth, but because it came to be in this place, it is beneficent, and because it is seen by that one, the same one becomes maleficent; and when again it deviates a little from the configuration, immediately it forgets its wickedness? And these things to this extent. But if at each indivisible moment of time they are changed to one configuration and another, and in these ten thousand changes, often in a day, the configurations of royal nativities are completed, why are kings not born every day? Or why are there at all paternal successions of kingships among them? For surely each of the kings does not, by careful observation, fit the birth of his own son to the royal configuration of the stars. For who among humans is master of such a thing? How then did Uzziah beget Jotham? Jotham Ahaz? Ahaz Hezekiah? And did no one among these meet with a servile hour of birth? Then if the beginnings of the activities according to vice and virtue are not from what is in our power, but the necessities are from nativity, the lawmakers are superfluous, who define what we must do and what we must avoid, and the judges are superfluous too, who honor virtue and punish wickedness. For the injustice is not the thief's; nor the murderer's; for whom it was not possible even if he wished to control his hand, because of the inescapable necessity pressing him toward the deeds.

choices.why: The image is of fragile, insubstantial webs that trap only the weak; 'spider webs' preserves the concrete image Basil uses to mock astrological arguments.
Basil uses this term for the human faculty of deliberate moral choice, central to his argument that virtue and vice are in our power, not determined by stars.
These are technical astrological terms for stars that supposedly bring good or evil fortune; Basil uses them ironically, and the English pair preserves the technical register.
This is the astrological term for an unfavorable position or lot; 'evil fortune' keeps the technical sense of a bad astrological placement.
Basil argues that if stars were evil by choice, they would have to be beings capable of deliberate choice, which is absurd for soulless bodies; 'creatures with choice' renders the phrase literally.
The word means 'unavoidable' or 'that cannot be run away from'; 'inescapable' captures the force of necessity Basil attributes to the astrological view he is refuting.

bible_refs.note: Uzziah (Azariah) begetting Jotham, Jotham Ahaz, Ahaz Hezekiah; Basil cites the royal succession to refute astrological determinism.

pass_b_english: But these clever arguments of theirs are like spider webs: when a gnat or a fly or some other weak creature of that kind gets caught in them, it is held fast; but when one of the stronger animals comes near, it slips through easily and tears the flimsy webs apart and destroys them.

And they do not stop at these things alone. Even the things over which each of us has authority by our own choice—I mean the pursuits of virtue or vice—even these they connect to causes in the heavens. To argue against them in any other way would be laughable, but because so many people are already held captive by the deception, it is perhaps necessary not to pass over it in silence.

First, then, let us ask them this: do not the configurations of the stars change countless times every day? For the so-called planets are always in motion, and some overtake one another more quickly, while others make their circuits more slowly, and at the same hour they often both see one another and are hidden from one another. And the greatest power in nativities, as they themselves say, lies in whether a person is watched over by a beneficent star or a maleficent one. And often, when they fail to discover the exact moment at which the beneficent star was bearing witness, because of ignorance of one of the smallest details, they record the person as lying under evil fortune. For I am compelled to use their own words.

In such arguments there is much foolishness, and far more impiety. For the maleficent stars transfer the cause of their own wickedness to the one who made them. If their evil comes from their nature, then the Creator will be the maker of evil. But if they become evil by choice, then first of all they will be creatures with choice, using free and self-governing impulses—which is beyond madness to attribute falsely to soulless things. And then how irrational it is: evil and good are not distributed to each according to merit, but because a star happens to be in a certain place, it is beneficent, and because it is seen by another star, the same one becomes maleficent; and again, when it shifts a little from its configuration, it immediately forgets its wickedness.

But let this be enough on those points. If at every indivisible moment of time the stars are rearranged into one configuration after another, and in these countless changes, many times a day, the configurations that produce royal nativities are completed, why are kings not born every day? Or why do they have hereditary successions of kingdoms at all? For surely each king does not carefully arrange the birth of his own son to fit the royal configuration of the stars. What human being has control over such a thing? How then did Uzziah beget Jotham, Jotham Ahaz, Ahaz Hezekiah? And in none of these did anyone happen upon a servile hour of birth?

Furthermore, if the origins of our actions in vice and virtue are not within our power, but the necessities come from our nativity, then lawmakers are superfluous, defining what we should do and what we should avoid; and judges are superfluous too, honoring virtue and punishing wickedness. For the theft is not the thief's fault, nor the murder the murderer's—since it was not possible for him, even if he wanted to, to control his hand, because of the inescapable necessity driving him to the deed.

problems.quote: the configurations of royal nativities are completed
problems.source_quote: οἱ τῶν βασιλικῶν γενέσεων ἀποτελοῦνται σχηματισμοὶ
problems.why: Subject and verb misread: 'the configurations of royal nativities are completed' reverses sense; Greek means 'the configurations that produce royal nativities are completed/result'.
problems.fix: configurations producing royal births are realized
problems.ruling: οἱ σχηματισμοὶ ἀποτελοῦνται = 'configurations are completed'; τῶν βασιλικῶν γενέσεων is genitive, not 'that produce.'

edits.old: the configurations of royal nativities are completed
edits.new: the configurations that produce royal nativities are completed

fixed: Corrected mistranslation: source 'οἱ τῶν βασιλικῶν γενέσεων ἀποτελοῦνται σχηματισμοὶ' means 'the configurations of royal nativities are completed' in the sense that the configurations produce the royal nativities, not that the nativities themselves are completed. Changed to 'the configurations that produce royal nativities are completed'.

last_rejected.why: Source says 'the same one becomes maleficent'; English omits 'the same one' (τὸν αὐτόν), losing the point that one and the same star changes nature.
last_rejected.ruling: English 'the same one' renders τὸν αὐτόν clearly; 'same one' is present.

last_rejected.why: Subject is wrong: the star is not forgetting its own wickedness, but the astrologers forget/ignore the star's wickedness.
last_rejected.fix: it is immediately forgotten as wicked
last_rejected.ruling: Subject is the star throughout; ἐπιλανθάνεσθαι fits 'forgets' its wickedness when configuration shifts.

last_rejected.quote: because it is seen by another star
last_rejected.why: Misreads ὁρᾶται: the star is 'watched over by' or 'aspected by' another star (astrological technical term), not merely 'seen by'.
last_rejected.fix: because it is aspected by another star
last_rejected.ruling: ὁρᾶται 'seen by' is within normal range; 'aspected by' is a preference, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: the configurations that produce royal nativities are completed
last_rejected.source_quote: οἱ τῶν βασιλικῶν γενέσεων ἀποτελοῦνται σχηματισμοί
last_rejected.why: Misreads grammar: the configurations are 'completed/fulfilled' (passive), not 'that produce royal nativities' (active).
last_rejected.fix: the configurations of royal nativities are completed
last_rejected.ruling: ἀποτελοῦνται can mean 'are completed/produced'; rendering as 'produce' is within acceptable range.

last_rejected.quote: And in none of these did anyone happen upon a servile hour of birth
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐν τούτοις δουλικῇ συνέτυχεν ὥρᾳ γενέσεως
last_rejected.why: Subject wrong: 'no one encountered a servile hour of birth among these'—meaning none of these kings had a servile horoscope, not that no one 'happened upon' it.
last_rejected.fix: and none of these encountered a servile hour of birth
last_rejected.ruling: συνέτυχεν ὥρᾳ 'happen upon a servile hour' correctly conveys none of these kings had a servile horoscope.

last_rejected.quote: For the theft is not the thief's fault, nor the murder the murderer's
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐ γὰρ τοῦ κλέπτου τὸ ἀδίκημα· οὐδὲ τοῦ φονέως
last_rejected.why: Wrong sense: ἀδίκημα is 'unjust act/crime', not 'fault' or 'blame'; the claim is the crime belongs to the thief, not that it doesn't.
last_rejected.fix: For the crime is the thief's; the murder too is the murderer's
last_rejected.ruling: ἀδίκημα as 'fault' conveys the argument: the crime is not the thief's own doing under determinism.

last_rejected.quote: since it was not possible for him, even if he wanted to, to control his hand
last_rejected.source_quote: ᾧ γε οὐδὲ βουλομένῳ δυνατὸν ἦν κρατεῖν τῆς χειρὸς
last_rejected.why: Wrong referent: ᾧ refers back to the murderer (dative of possession/reference), but the logic is inverted—the text says 'for whom not even when willing was it possible to control his hand', i.e., astrological determinism makes this so.
last_rejected.fix: for whom it was not possible, even if willing, to control his hand
last_rejected.ruling: Translation correctly captures ᾧ: 'not possible for him, even if he wanted to, to control his hand'—no inversion.

last_rejected.source_quote: μεγίστην τε ἔχει δύναμιν ἐν ταῖς γενέσεσι
last_rejected.why: Missing 'as they themselves say' (ὡς αὐτοὶ λέγουσι) which marks this as the astrologers' claim, not Basil's.
last_rejected.fix: and, as they themselves say, the greatest power in nativities
last_rejected.ruling: ὡς αὐτοὶ λέγουσι appears in next sentence ('For I am compelled to use their own words'), not omitted.
